newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS - Spain, Portugal plan to join euro from start.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain, Portugal plan to join euro from start.

text.p: Spain and Portugal are determined to join the planned European single currency from the start, Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres said on Wednesday.

"There is a firm determination to ensure that Portugal and Spain will be among the founder nations of the single currency," Guterres told a news conference, winding up a two-day summit with his Spanish counterpart Jose Maria Aznar in the Azores.
"This summit took place in a climate of great confidence and friendship," Guterres said.
Discussions of the two states' ambitions to join the single currency, or euro, from the start dominated the summit.
Portugal and Spain want solidarity among European Union (EU) states in terms of attitudes to the euro, Guterres said.
Guterres said Portugal was on course to meet economic targets to join the euro, due to be launched in January 1999.
Officials ruled out any delay in the timetable for its launch.
Guterres said: "I believe Portugal's economic indicators show that Portugal is meeting Maastricht criteria consistently."

The Maastricht Treaty on European economic and monetary union requires countries meet a series of economic targets, including reducing their budget deficits to no more than three percent of gross domestic product in 1997.

Portuguese budget proposals, now being considered by parliament, forecast that the budget deficit will drop to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, within the three-percent goal, from around four percent this year.
Talks between officials of the two countries ranged from bilateral issues such as scarce water resources to international matters, including the EU summit in Dublin in December.
Spanish officials expressed support for Portugal's efforts to win self-determination for the people of the former Portuguese colony of East Timor.
"Spain has supported Portugal in its campaign in favour of Timor and this was reaffirmed again here," a Portuguese government source said.

Portuguese President Jorge Sampaio said this week he would accept an offer to head a Lisbon-based foundation supporting East Timor's independence cause, which is to be created by Nobel laureate Jose Ramos-Horta.

East Timor has been in turmoil since Indonesia invaded it in 1975. The United Nations does not recognise Indonesian sovereignty and considers Portugal, the former colonial power, as the administering power.
Officials from both countries discussed judicial and police coooperation in the war on terrorism and drug trafficking.
The two police forces are struggling to contain increasingly powerful and innovative drug gangs which run cocaine, heroin and cannabis into Spain and Portugal by land and sea.
Portugal congratulated Spain on the appointment of Spaniard Miguel Angel Moratinos as the EU's special envoy to the Middle East, officials added.
